examples: The teacher gave me a book.
My father gave me a watch.
fields.explain:
くれます is used only when someone else gives something to you (or to your family members ちち、はは、あね、あに、おとうと、いもうと…)
わたしに can be omitted as follows:
N 1 が　Nを　くれました
fields.notes:
explain: Use が for the giver and に for the receiver (me/my group): N が私に N を くれます。
Do not use くれる if the receiver is not on my side (use あげる instead).
In conversation, くれた (casual past) is common:友だちがくれた。
examples: 1. 友だちが私にプレゼントをくれました。
My friend gave me a present.
2. 母が私に新しい靴をくれました。
My mother gave me new shoes.
3. 会社が私に休みをくれました。
The company gave me a day off.
4. 田中さんが妹に本をくれました。
Mr. Tanaka gave my younger sister a book.
5. 先生が私に日本語を教えてくれます。
My teacher teaches me Japanese.
explain: Casual and familiar; suitable for diaries, conversation, and personal expressions of thanks.
“私に” is usually omitted when it is obvious that the receiver is me:友だちがプレゼントをくれた。
With abstract nouns such as アドバイス/情報: “アドバイスをくれる” is more natural than “アドバイスをあげる”.
At work, toward superiors/customers: prefer くださる/いただく.
examples: 1. 友だちが私に手作りのクッキーをくれた。
My friend gave me homemade cookies.
2. 父が弟に新しい自転車をくれた。
My father gave my younger brother a new bicycle.
3. 先生が娘に絵本をくれた。
The teacher gave my daughter a picture book. (the receiver is on my side)
4. 彼が私に誕生日プレゼントをくれた。
He gave me a birthday present.
5. （対比）彼が私に本をくださった。
Same content, but showing respect to the giver (くださる).
6. （×）彼が田中さんに本をくれた→彼が田中さんに本をあげた。
(Correction) The receiver is not on my side → use あげる.
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Short example
N をくれる | Gives to me/my group | Casual | 友人（ゆうじん）が花（はな）をくれた
N をくださる | (A superior) gives to me | Keigo form of くれる | 先生（せんせい）が本（ほん）をくださった
N をもらう | I receive | Neutral | 友人（ゆうじん）から花（はな）をもらった
N をいただく | I receive (humble) | Very polite | 先生（せんせい）から本（ほん）をいただいた
N をあげる | I give to someone | Giver's point of view | 私（わたし）は彼（かれ）に花（はな）をあげた
N をください | Asking (please give) | Request sentence | 領収（りょうしゅう）書（しょ）をください
Vてくれる | Does V for me | Related verb pattern | 手伝（てつだ）ってくれる
common_mistakes: • Using くれる when the receiver is not on your side: incorrect. Fix: あげる/与える.
• Using くれる with a superior as the giver in formal language: switch to くださる/いただく.
• Confusing particle positions: “X が 私に N を くれる” (not 私がXに…くれる).
• Dropping “に” for the receiver in a long sentence: this easily makes subject, verb and object ambiguous.
meaning_vi: Expresses receiving the transfer of ownership from the other party. The verbs 「あげる．もらう．くれる」all have the meaning
examples: 1. ①　あなたが　くれたんでしょう。
You gave it to me, didn't you?
2. ②　わたしは　かのじょに　指輪を　あげました。
I gave my girlfriend a ring.
3. ➂　かのじょは　わたしに　時計を　くれました。
My girlfriend gave me a watch.
4. ➃　わたしは　かのじょに　時計を　もらいました。
I received a watch from my girlfriend.
mistakes: Confusing roles: ×私が田中さんに本をくれました → it should be私が田中さんに本をあげました。
Omitting にfor the receiver: ×友だちが私本をくれました → correct:私に本をくれました。
Using くれる when the receiver is not on my side: ×田中さんが鈴木さんに本をくれました → use あげました instead。

examples: This is the meeting room.
That over there is the hospital.
fields.explain:
ここ、そこ、あそこ or こちら、そちら、あちら：Used to refer to places.
Of these, こちら、そちら、あちら are the polite way of saying ここ、そこ、あそこ. In addition, こちら、そちら、あちら are also used to refer to directions.

ここ：This place, here
そこ：That place, there
あそこ：That place over there, over there
→　Question word　どこ：Where?
こちら：This way
そちら：That way
あちら：That way over there
→　Question word　どちら：Where, which way, which direction?

fields.meaning: そうですか　I see (Is that so).
examples:
A: Is this umbrella yours?
B: No, it isn't. It's Ms. Sato's.
A: I see.
fields.explain:
Used when the speaker receives some information and shows that they have understood it.
Even though there is か at the end of the sentence, it is not a question but an exclamation.
そうですか is pronounced with a falling intonation at the end of the sentence.

fields.meaning: そうですね　That's right (Yes, indeed).
examples:
A: Tomorrow is a day off, isn't it?
B: Oh, that's right.
fields.explain:
そうですね　expresses agreement or sympathy with what the other person says.
そうですね　agrees or sympathizes with something one thinks or knows # そうですか takes in new information one did not know .

examples: This cake is delicious. And it's cheap.
Mt. Fuji is beautiful. And it's famous.
I'm a university student. And I also have a part-time job.
I got up in the morning. Then I took a shower.
Japanese food is delicious. And it's also good for your health.
He is smart. And he is very kind.
fields.explain:
“そして” is a conjunction with a natural, neutral nuance, used to narrate, present or explain.
It can be used both in casual speech and in formal written language.
When joining two clauses with the same subject or the same topic, “そして” makes the sentence more coherent and easier to understand.
Unlike “それで” (cause – result), “そして” only joins events in a sequence or as a listing.

“そして” is used tojoin two sentences in a sequential relationship or to add information.
Basic meaning:“and”, “then”, “moreover”.
Used in spoken and written language, it expresses a natural link between two actions, events or ideas.
Unlike “それから” (which focuses on time sequence), “そして” can also join clauses related in content or carry emphasis.
fields.notes:
“そして” often appears in narratives or descriptions of a series of events.
In casual conversation, “そして” is sometimes omitted by Japanese speakers or replaced with “で” or “それで”.
In formal written language, “そして” makes sentences coherent and natural without being too stiff.
At JLPT N5, it is one of the most basic conjunctions to remember when writing paragraphs or joining sentences.
mistakes: Confusing it with “それで”:“そして” only joins events or ideas; “それで” expresses cause – result.
Wrong position:“そして” usually joins two independent sentences and is not used between two clauses within one short sentence.
Writing it in kanji by mistake:“そして” is always written in hiragana; it has no kanji form.
JLPT N5 often tests choosing the correct conjunction among “そして”, “それから” and “それで”.

rows: Joins two sentences on the same topic, adding information or a sequence
パンを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べました。そしてコーヒーを<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>みました。

<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>医者<rt>いしゃ</rt></ruby>です。そしてまた<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>でもあります。

examples: It's very cold in Beijing.
This dish is very delicious.
Yesterday was a lot of fun.
fields.explain:
とても further emphasizes the quality expressed by the adjective
あまり goes with a negative ending and softens the meaning

～とても～：　very ~
～あまり～ない：　not very ~.

fields.name: なん and なに
fields.meaning: なん and なに are both question words with the same meaning, “what”
fields.connection: なに/なん + particle (何を/何が/何の N) / なん + [counter] (なんじ・なんにん…)
examples: What book is it?
How old is Teresa?
What will you eat?
I received a watch from my father.
Nam received a dictionary from the teacher.
fields.explain:
Someone received something from someone.
もらいます is not used to say that another person received something from you.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: Receive from (someone, a source)
explain: から emphasizes “from which source”: it can be used with people, organizations and places (先生から・会社から・銀行から・学校から…).
With a specific person, に is also natural:私は友だち に プレゼントをもらいました。
When the receiver is me/my group, もらう suits speaking from the “receiving” point of view.
Formal language/records usually use から; in everyday conversation both に and から occur.
examples: 1. 私は先生から本をもらいました。
I received a book from my teacher.
2. 会社からメールをもらいました。
I got an email from the company.
3. 昨日、友だちから電話をもらいました。
Yesterday I got a call from a friend.
4. 弟は近所の人からお菓子をもらいました。
My younger brother got some sweets from a neighbor.
5. 私は両親からお金をもらいません。
I don't take money from my parents.
6. これは田中さんからのプレゼントです。
This is a present from Mr. Tanaka.
explain: Prefer に with a specific person/organization; から is used to emphasize “from the side of” or the source (父から・会社から・国から).
V-て もらいます is often used to talk about “asking for help/being helped”. More polite when asking: V-て もらえますか／V-て いただけますか (very polite).
Subject: when the receiver is not the speaker, state it clearly to avoid ambiguity (例:弟は先生に本をもらいました).
The nuance of gratitude/receiving a favor is stronger in V-て もらう than in simply “receiving an object”.
examples: 1. 私は友だちに花をもらいました。
I received flowers from a friend.
2. 姉にお金をもらいませんでした。
I didn't receive any money from my older sister.
3. 先生に漢字を教えてもらいます。
My teacher teaches me kanji.
4. 田中さんからメールをもらいましたか。— はい、もらいました。
Did you get an email from Mr. Tanaka? — Yes, I did.
5. 友だちに宿題を手伝ってもらいました。
My friend helped me with my homework.
6. 母に新しい靴をもらいました。
I got new shoes from my mother.
7. 先生にもう一度説明してもらえますか。
Could you explain it once more, please?
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Key difference | Short example
N に N を もらう | Receive an object | Receiver's point of view | 私（わたし）は友（とも）だちに本（ほん）をもらった。
N に V-て もらう | Have someone do something for you | Emphasizes the favor/help | 母（はは）に送（おく）ってもらう。
N が 私（わたし）に N を くれる | Someone gives to me | Receiver's point of view but uses くれる | 友（とも）だちが私（わたし）に本（ほん）をくれた。
私（わたし）は N に N を あげる | I give to someone | Giver's point of view | 私（わたし）は弟（おとうと）に本（ほん）をあげた。
V-て くれる | Someone does something for me | Equivalent in meaning to V-て もらう, but the subject is “the doer” | 友（とも）だちが手伝（てつだ）ってくれた。
common_mistakes: Wrong particle for the giver: using を instead of に/から. Correct:友だちに/から本をもらう.
Confusing the point of view with くれる/あげる. Identify “who is the receiver”.
Forgetting the object marker を when receiving an object:私は彼にを× →私は彼に手紙をもらいました.
Using もらいます to say “I give to someone” is incorrect. In that case it must be あげます.
Requests that are not polite enough: × V-て もらいますか → use もらえますか/いただけますか.
explain: Used when the speaker is in the position of the receiver or represents the receiver (their family, their group).
Polite: もらいます； plain: もらう； past: もらった； potential: もらえる.
Gentle, neutral . Depending on the context, it can express gratitude.
In humble language, いただく can be used instead of もらう.
examples: 1. 先生に本をもらいました。
I received a book from my teacher.
2. 母から手紙をもらった。
I got a letter from my mother.
3. 誕生日に友だちにケーキをもらった。
On my birthday, I got a cake from a friend.
4. 会社からボーナスをもらいました。
I received a bonus from the company.
5. 兄は外国人の友達に日本のお土産をもらった。
My older brother got a Japanese souvenir from a foreign friend.
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Example
N を もらう | Receive something from someone | The speaker is the receiver | 友（とも）だちに本（ほん） をもらう
N を くれる | Someone gives to me | Giver → me (receiver's point of view) | 友（とも）だちが本（ほん） をくれる
N を あげる | I give to someone | Me → another person (giver's point of view) | 私（わたし）が友（とも）だちに本（ほん） をあげる
N を いただく | Receive humbly | More polite than もらう | 先生（せんせい）に本（ほん） をいただきました
common_mistakes: • Wrong particle: it must be N（giver）に N を もらう; から is not used in formal written language (but it is fine in conversation).
• Confusing it with くれる (the subject – target relationship is reversed).
• JLPT often tests distinguishing the three patterns: あげる・くれる・もらう.
meaning_vi: Expresses receiving the transfer of ownership from the other party.
examples: 1. ①　姉に　この　服を　もらいました。
I got these clothes from my older sister.
2. ②　なおきくんに　ラブレターを　もらいました。
I got a love letter from Naoki.
3. ③　たんじょう日に　だれかに　プレゼントを　もらいましたか。
Did you get a present from anyone on your birthday?
4. ④　これ、母に　もらったんです。とても　べんりです。
I got this from my mother. It's very handy.
mistakes: Wrong role marker: ×私は田中さんをプレゼントをもらいました → correct:私は田中さんから（に）プレゼントをもらいました。
Confusing the direction of giving/receiving: ×私は田中さんにプレゼントをもらいました (correct) but if it means “I gave”, you must use あげます, not もらいます.
Forgetting を for the object: ×先生から本もらいました → correct:本をもらいました。
Using から after私is unnatural if it means “from me”: ×私からもらいました (I received from myself) → meaningless.

examples: Let's take a short break.
Let's watch a movie together.
Let's do our best tomorrow, too.
Let's hurry home.
Let's think about it once more.
It's dangerous, so let's make sure not to go.
fields.explain:
Often used to invite, encourage, or suggest that others do something together.
It can go with “一緒に” to emphasize a shared action: 一緒に行きましょう。
When said to oneself (not including others), it means determination: もう泣くのをやめましょう。 → Let's stop crying now (said to oneself).
Unlike 「～てください」 (a request to others), 「～ましょう」 expresses a gentle invitation / suggestion.

① Suggesting / inviting the listener to do something together:Expresses the wish to invite or suggest doing an action together.
→ “Let's…”, “Let us…”.
② Expressing the speaker's volition or determination:When used alone (with no listener taking part), it means “I will…”, “Let's do it!”.
③ More formal and more polite than the imperative form:It is a soft way to invite or suggest, usable in polite conversation or announcements.
fields.notes:
The form～ましょうis the polite form of the volitional form (Vよう).
In conversation, “～ましょうか？” is used tooffer helpor ask for someone's opinion:例：手伝いましょうか？→ Shall I help?
The negative forms “～ないでおきましょう” or “～やめましょう” express a suggestion not to do something.
mistakes: Wrong verb form: you must conjugate to the ます form → ましょう(✕行くましょう → ○行きましょう).
Confusing it with 「Vませんか」:
“Vましょう” = an active suggestion to do something together,
“Vませんか” = an invitation that asks for the listener's opinion.
Forgetting the politeness nuance: “Vよう” is casual, “Vましょう” is polite.
JLPT N5 often tests distinguishing “Vましょう”, “Vませんか” and “Vてください”.

rows: Used in spoken language, between friends

examples: Hana, won't you come too?
Would you like to come over to my place this weekend?
Shall we have a nice, relaxed talk?
Are there any questions?
Would you like to watch a movie together?
Would you like some coffee?
fields.explain:
This sentence pattern is used to invite others to do an action together.
Vませんか here does not have a negative meaning.
We use Vませんか to invite when we do not know whether the other person will agree.
When accepting the invitation positively, we answer with Vましょう。

Meaning: “Would you like to…?”, used to invite someone politely.
The focus is on the listener: asking their opinion and respecting their decision.
Usable in most settings from casual to polite; safe in communication.
fields.notes:
For an even more polite invitation, you can use いかがですか with a noun: コーヒーはいかがですか。
Polite responses: はい、いいですね／すみません、今日はちょっと…。
It does not combine directly with adjectives/nouns; an action verb is required.
mistakes: Wrong conjugation: ×行くませんか → ✓行きませんか.
Using it to offer help (wrong function): to offer to open the door, use開けましょうか, not開けませんか.
Without一緒に the invitation can be ambiguous in some contexts; add一緒に to make the meaning “do together” clear.

rows: <ruby>公園<rt>こうえん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きませんか。
<ruby>公園<rt>こうえん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きましょう。

fields.name: ～か（listing: A or B）
examples: Orange or yellow
I want to go to the sea or the mountains this weekend.
Let's meet on Monday, Friday or Saturday!
Let's ask Mr. Yamada or Mr. Honda to do this.
How to use
It's easy to make.
fields.explain:
When the pitch falls at the end of the sentence, it is not a question but shows that new information from the speaker has been taken in.
Same as in the case of そうですか.

A particle that joins a noun with another noun. It expresses giving several options.

fields.name: ～から（reason）
examples: Sorry I'm late. It's because the train was delayed.
I'm taking today off. It's because I have a fever.
It's dangerous, so please don't go in.
I think that's necessary. It's because it's cheap and convenient.
It's raining, so let's stay home today.
I like Japanese, so I want to study abroad in Japan.
fields.explain:
The reason clause usually comes first and the result after. The sentence can be split when emphasizing the reason: ～。～から。
In formal settings/toward superiors, prefer ～ので／～ため(に) over ～から to avoid sounding rude/pushy.
～からだ at the end of a sentence is used to answer “why”: どうして？―忙しい からだ。

Expresses “because/that is because …” when stating a cause directly and concisely.
Often used as an independent explanatory sentence, after the result sentence or a question.
Neutral nuance; easy to use in everyday conversation and basic emails.
fields.notes:
With i形容詞/verbs: [Plain] + からです. With nouns/na形容詞: N/na + だ + からです (polite: ～だからです).
In an apology email: ご迷惑をおかけしました。確認が遅れたからです。
If you want to sound softer in formal settings, consider ～のでです／～ためです (beyond N5).
mistakes: Forgetting だ with な/名: ×静かから→ ○静かだから; ×学生から→ ○学生だから.
Using ～から too directly with superiors; switch to ～ので／～ため.
Confusing the order of information: reason first, result after within one sentence; if reversed, use からだ/なぜなら for clarity.

rows: Often used as an independent answer
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きません。<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいからです。
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>ですから、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きません。
Used with N/na<ruby>形容詞<rt>けいようし</rt></ruby>: N/na + だから
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>だから、<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い／<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>だからです。
N4; more polite and objective than ～から
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>なので、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きません。

examples: The bus is cheap, but it isn't convenient.
This tea is expensive, but it's delicious.
This shop is small, but it's very famous.
Japanese is difficult, but it's interesting.
It's cheap, but the quality is good.
Excuse me, but could you say that once more, please?
fields.explain:
Put “が” between two complete clauses; there is usually a comma: ～が、～.
Polite/neutral tone; for a strong contrast, use でも/しかし.
In emails/argumentative writing, ～が creates a gentle transition.

A
Expresses the subject of an action or event (in some cases a question word). Often used to talk about things happening right in front of you, as in the example, or to say that it is not something else, as in the example.
B
Often appears in the sentence pattern ～は～が。。。To express a part of the topic, as in example ①, or the target of ability, sensation or emotion, as in examples ②③④.
fields.notes:
Polite opening expressions:恐れ入りますが／失礼ですが／申し訳ありませんが.
In long complex sentences, the second clause can be omitted when the context is clear: すみませんが、明日… (implying “it's difficult/not possible”).
mistakes: Confusing the clause-joining “が” with the subject “が”: check whether there are two clauses, a first clause and a second clause.
Putting “でも” between clauses as in “XでもY” easily gives the wrong nuance; when joining clauses directly, use “が/けど”.
Overusing “が” can make sentences roundabout; for a strong contrast, switch to “しかし/でも”.

rows: But (at the beginning of a sentence)
しかし、<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>がある
